---
title: "2 · Random Matrix Theory"
---

A quantum system with no integrable structure has energy levels that look
erratic, yet their fine-grained statistics are reproducible. Across nuclei,
quantum billiards, and disordered conductors, the spacing distribution of
neighbouring levels matches that of a random matrix sharing the system's
symmetries, the content of the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit conjecture. Random matrix
theory supplies the reference distributions and explains why they are universal.

The mechanism is level repulsion. Changing variables from matrix entries to
eigenvalues produces a Jacobian carrying a factor of the squared eigenvalue
differences, which suppresses configurations with near-degenerate levels. The
power with which that factor vanishes is fixed by the time-reversal and
spin-rotation symmetry of the ensemble, giving exponents $1$, $2$, and $4$ for
the orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic classes. This part derives the Wigner
surmise from the two-by-two case, computes the semicircle density through its
moments and the Catalan numbers that count them, and introduces the gap-ratio
statistic that diagnoses chaos without the spectral unfolding that raw level
spacings require.

One caution about the surmise. It is exact only for $2\times2$ matrices; its
accuracy at large dimension is an empirical near-coincidence rather than the true
large-$N$ spacing law. This is part of why the gap ratio, which is insensitive to
the local mean level density, is often preferred in practice.

## Notebooks in this part

- [Level repulsion in the GOE](../notebooks/ch2/solution_ch2_goe_spacing.ipynb), deriving the Wigner surmise for nearest-neighbour spacings.
- [Moments of the Wigner semicircle](../notebooks/ch2/solution_ch2_semicircle_moments.ipynb), the Catalan-number combinatorics behind the density.
- [Eigenphase repulsion in the CUE](../notebooks/ch2/solution_ch2_cue_eigenphase.ipynb), the same physics for unitaries on the circle.
